newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech finmin says crown level good for medium term.
newsitem.headline: Czech finmin says crown level good for medium term.

text.p: Czech Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said on Friday that the Czech crown, after a recent sharp drop, was currently at a level which could be good for the economy in the medium term.

"If the exchange rate stabilises on more or less this level, the impact on the economy could be, in the medium-term also a good one," Pilip said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

"Of course it will have its negative impacts on the economy, including inflation and the prices of imported goods, but on the other hand, it is one of the ways to improve the conditions for our trade balance," Pilip said.

The Czech crown came under heavy speuclative pressure in late May by investors alarmed at a ballooning trade deficit and political instability, forcing the central bank to float the currency on May 27.

The crown has lost nearly 11 percent of its value against its previous mark/dollar peg, and some analysts expect the currency to weaken further once the central bank's prohibitively high interest rates, hiked to defend the crown, are eased.

The floating of the currency was followed by the announcement of an austerity programme of budget cuts and wage freezes along with a cabinet reshuffle which included installing Pilip, the former education minister, as finance minister.
But the foreign exchange markets have been anxiously awaiting a parliamentary vote of confidence in the cabinet, possibly to come on Tuesday, as a signal of where the crown may go next.

Asked if the economy could live with the high interest rates for long, Pilip said: "Definitely not for so many days or weeks, but now we feel that we must also stabilise the political situation that has developed with the pressure on the Czech crown."
The ruling three-party coalition holds 100 of the 200 seats in the lower house for the vote requiring a simple majority for approval, with the opposition holding 98 seats.
The votes of two independent deputies may determine the fate of the government.

"Next week on Tuesday there should be a confidence vote and we think that if we pass as a reconstructed government, that there is more space for some further steps concerning also the Czech crown because it plays a very important role," Pilip said.
Pilip said the government was ready to take steps in fiscal policy "to restrict the pressure on inflation because it could have a bad influence on the exchange rate of the crown."

"We are ready to have discussions in the government next week are we are preparing some cuts in expenditures of the state budget in order not to have a deficit which threatens our economy," Pilip said without elaborating.

The government austerity programme aimed at slowing domestic demand and counteracting the inflationary effects of the crown's depreciation, called for budget cuts leading to a balanced 1997 budget and a surplus budget in 1998, but the ministers have yet to give details of the extent of the cuts.

Analysts have calculated the 1997 cuts, in addition to 25.5 billion crowns in cuts already announced in April, would have to be anywhere from 25 billion to 70 billion crowns to reach the government's goals.
After the April cuts, total 1997 expenditures were forecast at roughly 523 billion crowns.
